topic: NPCI Introduces MDR on UPI Transactions

subtopics.title: MDR framework and rates
subtopics.summary: NPCI has introduced a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework for eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions, effective from 15 October 2026. The main rate is 0.4 per cent of value for the mid-value slab. The zero-MDR policy introduced in 2020 had exempted merchants from paying any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions.
facts: Framework covers eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000
New framework comes into effect from 15 October 2026
MDR of 0.40% of value applies to the mid-value slab
High-value transactions of ₹75,000 and above are capped at ₹300 per transaction
Zero-MDR policy for UPI and RuPay was introduced in 2020
Zero-MDR policy aimed to encourage digital adoption among small businesses and informal sectors
MDR is a fee for processing a digital payment, borne by the merchant

subtopics.title: Exemptions, caps and special categories
subtopics.summary: Several categories of UPI payments are exempt from MDR, including person-to-person (P2P) transactions and P2M payments up to ₹2,000. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the P2PM category also remain exempt. Sector-specific payments and capital-market payments follow separate charging structures.
facts: P2P UPI transactions are not subject to MDR
P2M UPI payments up to ₹2,000 are exempt, including through RuPay debit cards
Transactions involving small vendors are exempt
Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month via UPI QR codes (P2PM) remain exempt
Railways, telecom, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs pay a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction above ₹2,000
Mutual funds, securities, stock brokers and stock dealers attract a reduced MDR of 0.02%
Capital-market payments are subject to a ₹300 cap
Lower capital-market rate is intended to encourage digital payments in formal financial markets

subtopics.title: Why MDR was introduced
subtopics.summary: The booklet lists several reasons for the MDR framework, centred on the financial sustainability of UPI. Revenue from the framework can fund infrastructure, cybersecurity and innovation. The framework also keeps P2P and low-value merchant payments free to protect consumers.
facts: UPI requires continuous investment in payment infrastructure and technology
Growing digital payments need stronger systems to prevent fraud and cyber threats
A revenue mechanism can support continued operation and expansion of UPI
Revenue can support technological improvements and new payment solutions
Framework keeps P2P payments and low-value merchant payments free
Eligible small merchants continue to receive zero-MDR benefits
A self-funded payment ecosystem can reduce dependence on continued public funding
Small merchants and ordinary users need protection from additional costs

subtopics.title: MDR, UPI and NPCI basics
subtopics.summary: MDR is a fee charged on digital payment transactions and borne by the merchant, and it is not a tax collected by the government. UPI is a real-time, 24/7 payment system that is accepted in 11 countries. NPCI was established in 2008 as a Section 8 company under the Companies Act 2013.
facts: MDR is distributed among banks, payment service providers and other relevant participants
MDR is not a tax collected by the government
MDR revenue remains within the payment ecosystem
UPI is a real-time, 24/7, instant and interoperable payment system
UPI is the world's largest retail fast payment system by transaction volume
UPI is accepted in 11 countries, including Greece, Singapore, France and Qatar
NPCI was established in 2008 as a Section 8 company under the Companies Act 2013
NPCI was set up as an initiative of the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association
NPCI's major payment systems are UPI, RuPay, IMPS and FASTag
NPCI's headquarters is in Mumbai, Maharashtra

quizzes.passage: The Unified Payments Interface has grown into a large digital payment network that handles billions of transactions every month. Running such a network requires continuous spending on technology, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, server capacity and customer support. Until now, merchants have not paid any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions, which helped small businesses and informal sectors adopt digital payments. As the network expands, however, planners must decide how its upkeep should be funded. The answer proposed in the new framework is a fee on certain merchant payments, while everyday low-value transactions remain free. Officials have stressed that small merchants and ordinary users should not face additional costs. The fee is therefore aimed at larger merchant payments rather than at the many small transactions that make up daily life. Such a structure lets the payment ecosystem generate revenue that supports its own operation. Policymakers have sought a balance between funding the network and protecting the people who use it every day. UPI works in real time and around the clock, connecting individuals and merchants across banks. Its wide use has made it an important part of commerce, from neighbourhood shops to large retailers. Because so many people rely on it, any change to how the network is priced affects a very large number of users and businesses.

quizzes.passage: Digital payments work best when small transactions stay cheap for everyone who uses them. Households send money to one another every day, and shopkeepers in local markets often accept payments through a QR code displayed at the counter. Many of these businesses operate on thin margins, so an extra charge on each small sale can matter a great deal. Policymakers have therefore tried to protect the smallest users while still asking larger participants to share the cost of running the network. The new approach separates payments into groups. Some payments remain free regardless of who sends or receives them, while others attract a charge only when they are large. Certain sectors that provide essential services are placed in a separate group, where a fixed charge per transaction applies rather than a percentage. Investments routed through mutual funds and securities are charged at a lower rate, because that rate is meant to encourage greater use of digital payments in formal financial markets. Several upper limits also protect users. A single ceiling prevents very large payments from carrying an unlimited fee, and small merchants who earn only modest amounts through QR codes each month are exempt from the charge altogether. Together, these rules aim to keep ordinary digital payments affordable while the payment infrastructure keeps growing.
